extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, literary theory, and humor research
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classification of conceptual joke techniques—what mechanical operations produce comic effect (e.g., unification, representation by the opposite, allusion, analogy). Useful for scholars or writers studying how jokes are constructed and why they produce certain reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Stringing things together (often with 'and') to imply a connection so the reader/listener perceives a unified category or relation where none legitimately exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique makes otherwise disparate items seem connected (e.g., Heine's 'students, professors, philistines and donkeys'), producing comic effect by the implied relation. Positioning (like placing 'caning' between two school subjects) can enhance the perceived connection. Useful for producing unsuspected analogies; undoing the unification removes the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joking enumeration (co-ordination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Listing items together in a way that creates a humorous implication by their grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumeration implies equivalence or relation among grouped elements; comedic force comes from an unexpected or disparaging item in the list (example: 'students, professors, philistines and donkeys'). Not all enumerations are jokes—placement and implied relations matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by the opposite
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing the expected negative answer or idea with its opposite (often 'yes' instead of 'no'), frequently tempered by a 'but' that restores the negative sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploits the cognitive expectation of a particular reply; e.g., replying 'Yes, but...' to mean 'No.' Produces surprise and comic reversal (examples: preacher conjuring spirits: 'At your Majesty’s command. But they don’t come.'). Can produce irony if used outside joke contexts. Technique alone does not fully define a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overstatement as inverted confirmation/denial
rubrics_metrics.description: Using an apparently opposite response (a denial or affirmation) whose content functions as an intensified form of the expected reply, so that a denial acts like an overstated 'yes' or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works by having a denial emphasize the quality it's denying (e.g., boasting about cleanliness to imply uncleanliness). Often traceable to representation by the opposite. Produces comic contrast between form and intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by something akin / Indirect representation (allusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing a meaning not directly but by pointing to something conceptually linked (allusion), including resemblance in sound, sentence pattern, or a shared structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusion can be via sound similarity (punning on phrases), partial structural similarity, omission of the linking thought, or condensation with modification. Examples: imitating proverbs ('New spas cure well' ~ 'New brooms sweep clean') or invoking an associated image (critic: 'Where’s the Saviour?' implying 'thieves' = rascals). Allusion is common and versatile, but on its own does not guarantee a joke—it must produce a comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion by modification (condensation with modification / substitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forming a witty phrase by slightly altering a familiar expression (letter change, word substitution) so the new phrase alludes to the original and suggests an unstated idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: wordplay changes like 'Dichteritis' (authoritis) or changing 'twelve moons' to 'twelve Moden' produce humor by echoing a known phrase while shifting meaning. This is close to puns but operates at the level of whole phrases or idioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allusion by omission
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving out an expected connective or explanatory thought so that the audience must infer the omitted material, yielding an allusive comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The joke depends on the audience filling the gap (e.g., 'If X hears of this, he'll get his ears boxed again'—omits 'he'll write a scathing article and so on'). Works well combined with nonsense or bewilderment to create a punchline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation (multiple use of same material / prolongation of analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-using or extending a familiar expression or analogy and then adding a further unexpected continuation, restoring force to a cliché or creating a new joke from recycled material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving a 'watered-down' expression back its full force by elaboration (e.g., reviving 'the torch of truth' with a concrete twist). Often interacts with unification and analogy; useful to refresh clichés into jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punning / verbal technique (sound resemblance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using similarity of sound between words or phrases (or between sentences/structures) to trigger a linked, often comic, meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not limited to single-word puns—can involve whole phrases or characteristic sentences that echo familiar utterances. Examples include letter/syllable-level echoes or deliberate slips that create double-meanings ('Round the Wilt in 80 Days').

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by something small (miniaturization/detail highlighting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing a large or full characteristic by reference to a tiny, telling detail which stands in for the whole, thereby producing a comic condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small action or sign can evoke an entire disposition (e.g., a traveller immediately putting feet back up when asked about Yom Kippur). Related to the 'tendency to economy'—using minimal cues for maximal meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A general principle where jokes economize expression—using small details, omissions, or brief substitutions to represent larger thoughts or chains of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why minimal signals (a gesture, a single word) can carry rich comic content; supports techniques like omission and representation by something small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy (joking analogies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using analogy to map one domain onto another in a way that produces amusement, often by surprising or incongruous correspondence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy-based jokes vary: some analogies are clearly jokes (especially when continued or prolonged into further unexpected consequences), while others are apt analogies without comic effect. Joking analogies often rely on unification, absurd juxtaposition, or extension of the analogy into consequences (e.g., 'reviews are a childish illness' then mapping book fates onto illness outcomes). Note: many analogies may not provoke explosive laughter and sometimes feel different from other joke types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by absurdity (absurd juxtaposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing humor by assigning surprising, bizarre, or incongruous epithets or attributes (juxtaposing high abstractions with low concretes), making the combination absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'learned entrails' or 'moral backside.' Often overlaps with analogy and debasing/disparaging effects. The absurdity of juxtaposition can itself be the vehicle of the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifting emphasis from the expected object or content to something else, so that a reply or attitude appears discordant with the demand of the situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often combines with representation-by-opposite (e.g., wax-work guide boasting propriety instead of identifying figures). Produces comic effect by the mismatch between situation and response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faulty reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using logically flawed or superficially absurd inferences as the basis for the punchline, where the laugh comes from recognizing and resolving the faulty chain of thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified by Freud alongside unification and indirect representation as a head category of conceptual joke techniques. The comic arises from the cognitive play with expected inference patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irony (technique overlap with jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation by the opposite used in non-joke contexts (e.g., rhetorical irony), sharing technique with jokes but distinct in tone and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes that technique (representation by opposite) is not sufficient to define jokes—irony uses the same mechanism but serves different literary ends. Be cautious: the presence of this technique does not automatically make a passage a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic effect depends on combination of techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Most effective jokes often combine multiple techniques (e.g., representation by opposite + displacement; allusion + omission + nonsense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolating a single technique may not capture why a joke works; analysts and creators should look for interacting mechanisms. Undoing the operative techniques typically removes the humor.
